description: The Last Supper, crucifixion, resurrection and ascension — and Christian beliefs about salvation and atonement.
content_html:
The Last Days of Jesus

The final events of Jesus’s earthly life are central to Christian faith. Luke 22–24 provides the primary Gospel account: the Last Supper, arrest, trial before Pilate, crucifixion, death, burial, resurrection and ascension. Christians regard these events not merely as historical facts but as the pivot of all human history: the moment God acted decisively to deal with sin and death.

At the Last Supper (Luke 22:7–23), Jesus took bread, broke it and said “This is my body given for you; do this in remembrance of me.” He took the cup of wine and called it “the new covenant in my blood.” Christians have interpreted this in different ways — from a symbolic memorial to a real transformation of the bread and wine — but all major denominations trace the Eucharist or Lord’s Supper back to this moment.

Key Fact

Luke 22–24 is the primary biblical anchor for Edexcel’s section on the last days of Jesus’s life. The sequence runs: Last Supper → betrayal and arrest → trial before the high priest and Pilate → crucifixion and death → burial → resurrection (the empty tomb, Luke 24:1–12) → appearances to disciples → ascension (Luke 24:50–53). Luke alone among the Gospels continues the story into Acts, making the ascension a key transition point.

The Crucifixion and Its Significance

Jesus was crucified outside Jerusalem. Christians believe that on the cross, Jesus took upon himself the consequence of human sin — separation from God, suffering and death. The crucifixion is not seen as a tragic accident but as the fulfilment of God’s saving plan. For many Protestant Christians this is expressed through penal substitution: Christ died in our place, bearing the penalty for sin. Other traditions emphasise different models, but all affirm that the cross has saving power.

Atonement means making amends for wrongdoing; in Christianity it refers to how Jesus’s death restores the broken relationship between humanity and God. Different traditions emphasise different aspects: Penal substitution (dominant in evangelical Protestantism): Jesus took the punishment humanity deserved. “God made him who had no sin to be sin for us, so that in him we might become the righteousness of God” (2 Corinthians 5:21). Moral influence / example theory: The cross shows the depth of God’s love, motivating humans to repent and change — associated with Abelard. Christus Victor: The cross is where Jesus defeats the powers of sin, death and the devil, liberating humanity. This resonates strongly in Eastern Orthodox and some Lutheran theology. All three models agree that the cross is salvific; they differ in explaining how. In a 12-mark Discuss, students can use this diversity as evidence that “atonement is not a straightforward concept even within Christianity.”

The Resurrection and Ascension

Christians believe that three days after the crucifixion, Jesus rose bodily from the dead. Luke 24 describes the empty tomb discovered by women, then appearances of the risen Jesus to disciples. The resurrection is considered the foundation of Christian faith: without it, the cross would simply be a tragedy. Paul writes in 1 Corinthians 15:17 that “if Christ has not been raised, your faith is futile.” For Christians, the resurrection demonstrates that Jesus was who he claimed to be, and that death is not the final word for those who follow him.

The ascension (Luke 24:50–53; Acts 1:9) is when the risen Jesus returned to the Father in heaven, forty days after the resurrection. Christians believe the ascension means Jesus now intercedes for believers at the right hand of God. It also prepares for Pentecost — the coming of the Holy Spirit — and gives the disciples their commission to take the message of Jesus to the whole world.

Salvation, Law, Sin and Grace

Salvation is the central purpose of the last days of Jesus’s life. Christian teaching on salvation involves several interlocking concepts. Law: the Old Testament law showed God’s standard and revealed human failure to meet it. Sin: every human being falls short of God’s standard, breaking the relationship with God. Grace: God’s free, undeserved gift of forgiveness and restored relationship, made available through Christ. Spirit: the Holy Spirit applies salvation to individual believers, assuring them of God’s love and enabling holy living.

Key Fact

John 3:10–21 (Jesus speaks to Nicodemus) teaches that those who believe in the Son of God will not perish but have eternal life — salvation is through belief. Acts 4:8–12 records Peter declaring: “Salvation is found in no one else, for there is no other name under heaven given to mankind by which we must be saved.” This text is used to support the claim that salvation is exclusively through Jesus Christ — a conviction shared across all major Protestant traditions and the wider Christian Church.

Grace and Sola Fide

Protestant Christianity places particular emphasis on sola fide (faith alone), a principle central to the Reformation. Luther, Calvin and other Reformers argued that salvation is entirely God’s gift — received through faith, not earned by human effort. This is grounded in passages like John 3:16 (“whoever believes in him shall not perish but have eternal life”). Catholic theology affirms that grace is essential but also teaches that faith expresses itself in works and sacraments. The disagreement about the precise relationship between faith, works and grace remains one of the significant historic differences between Protestant and Catholic Christianity, though dialogue since the 20th century has narrowed the gap considerably.

Protestant: Salvation is by grace alone (sola gratia) through faith alone (sola fide). Sacraments are important but do not themselves confer salvation — they are signs and seals of God’s grace received by faith. Baptism and the Lord’s Supper are the two sacraments commanded by Christ. Catholic: Salvation is by God’s grace, which is communicated through the seven sacraments (Catechism of the Catholic Church 1210–1211). Good works done in a state of grace are genuinely meritorious. The Church and its sacramental ministry play an integral role in applying Christ’s redemption. Orthodox: Salvation is understood as theosis (deification) — humans progressively participating in the divine nature through the life of the Church. All three traditions affirm that it is Christ’s death and resurrection that make salvation possible; the differences are in the mechanism of how that salvation reaches individual believers.
exam_tip_html: When answering a 5-mark ‘Explain two … including a reference to a source of wisdom and authority’ question on salvation, you must cite a named source. Good options for this topic: “Acts 4:8–12 states ‘Salvation is found in no one else’” or “John 3:10–21 teaches that belief in the Son brings eternal life.” A vague phrase like “the Bible teaches that Jesus saves us” without naming a passage will not earn the 5th mark. For 12-mark Discuss questions on the cross or resurrection, the most common error is spending all the space on one side (usually arguments supporting the statement) and leaving only a sentence for the other side. Examiners reward balance: develop at least two reasons on each side, each backed by a named teaching or scriptural source. SPaG marks on selected 12-mark questions reward correct use of specialist vocabulary: ‘atonement’, ‘salvation’, ‘resurrection’, ‘ascension’ must be spelt correctly.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • The last days of Jesus (Luke 22–24) include the Last Supper, betrayal, trial, crucifixion, resurrection and ascension — Christians believe these events are the means by which God saves humanity from sin and death.
  • Salvation involves law (revealing human failure), sin (breaking relationship with God), grace (God’s free forgiveness) and Spirit (applying salvation to believers); Acts 4:8–12 and John 3:10–21 are the key biblical anchors.
  • Protestant Christianity emphasises sola fide (salvation by faith alone); Catholic and Orthodox traditions affirm the role of sacraments and the Church in applying Christ’s salvation — all agree that the cross and resurrection are the source of salvation.

practice_questions.text: Outline three events in the last days of Jesus's life.
practice_questions.marks: One mark for each of three discrete, accurate points from: Last Supper, betrayal, arrest, trial before Pilate, crucifixion, death, burial, resurrection, ascension. Each must be a separate identifiable event — do not award a single mark for a narrative sentence covering multiple events.

practice_questions.text: Describe what Christians believe about the resurrection of Jesus.
practice_questions.marks:
Acceptable content:
- Jesus rose bodily from the dead on the third day after the crucifixion.
- The empty tomb was discovered by women followers, as described in Luke 24:1-12.
- The risen Jesus appeared to his disciples before his ascension.
- The resurrection is the foundation of Christian hope — without it Paul says 'your faith is futile' (1 Corinthians 15:17).
[1 mark per accurate point, up to 3]

practice_questions.text: Explain two ways in which the crucifixion is important for Christian beliefs about salvation.
practice_questions.marks:
Two developed explanations required.

Acceptable explanations:
- The crucifixion is where Christians believe Jesus took the penalty for human sin: through his death, the broken relationship between God and humanity is restored. This means the cross is not a defeat but the central act of God's saving plan.
- The crucifixion demonstrates the depth of God's love: Jesus was willing to suffer and die for sinners, showing that God's grace is freely given, not earned. This motivates Christians to respond in faith and gratitude rather than trying to earn their own salvation.
[2 marks per explanation: 1 for point, 1 for development]

practice_questions.text: Explain two Christian beliefs about salvation, including a reference to a source of wisdom and authority.
practice_questions.marks:
Two developed explanations (2 marks each) plus a named source (1 mark).

Acceptable explanations:
- Christians believe salvation is found exclusively in Jesus Christ: Peter declares in Acts 4:8-12 that 'Salvation is found in no one else, for there is no other name under heaven given to mankind by which we must be saved.' This means Christians believe faith in Jesus is the only route to restored relationship with God.
- Christians believe salvation is received through faith, not earned by human effort: John 3:10-21 records Jesus teaching Nicodemus that those who believe in the Son of God will not perish but have eternal life — a gift of God's grace (sola fide in Protestant tradition).

The 5th mark: the source must be named (Acts 4:8-12, John 3:10-21, or another specific reference). A vague phrase like 'the Bible teaches salvation' does not earn the 5th mark.

practice_questions.text:
'The resurrection is more important than the crucifixion for Christian faith.'
Discuss this statement.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (10-12): Both sides fully developed with named sources; explicit weighing of perspectives; justified conclusion.

Secure (7-9): Both sides present with some development; at least one named source; conclusion present.

Developing (4-6): One side more developed; limited sources; conclusion descriptive.

Emerging (1-3): One-sided; minimal development; no named sources.

Arguments in support (resurrection more important):
- Paul argues that the resurrection is the proof that Jesus is who he claimed to be and that the cross worked: 'If Christ has not been raised, your faith is futile; you are still in your sins' (1 Corinthians 15:17). Without the resurrection, the cross is merely a tragic death.
- The resurrection is the basis of Christian hope for life after death: because Jesus rose, Christians believe they too will rise. The ascension follows from the resurrection, giving Jesus his role as intercessor at God's right hand.
- Many Protestant theologians argue that Easter Sunday is more fundamental than Good Friday in the Christian calendar — the cross only makes sense in the light of the empty tomb.

Arguments against (crucifixion equally or more important):
- The cross is where the actual work of salvation takes place: Jesus bears the consequence of sin and makes reconciliation possible. Acts 4:8-12 and John 3:10-21 point to belief in the crucified Christ as the means of salvation — not the resurrection as a separate event.
- Many atonement theologies (penal substitution, Christus Victor, moral influence) are primarily focused on what happens at the cross, not the resurrection. The resurrection validates but does not replace the cross.
- Some Christians argue the two events are inseparable: the 'Paschal Mystery' (a Catholic term used across denominations) refers to both together as one saving event. Separating them misunderstands the doctrine.

SPaG note: 'resurrection', 'crucifixion', 'ascension', 'atonement' must be spelt correctly for SPaG marks.

practice_questions.text: Explain two differences between Protestant and Catholic beliefs about how salvation works.
practice_questions.marks:
Two developed explanations required.

Acceptable explanations:
- Protestants emphasise sola fide (faith alone): salvation is received through faith in Christ, not through performing sacraments or good works. Catholics teach that grace is communicated through the seven sacraments (CCC 1210-1211) and that works done in grace are genuinely meritorious.
- Protestants generally recognise two sacraments (baptism and the Lord's Supper/Eucharist), commanded by Jesus in the Gospels. Catholics recognise seven sacraments as channels of grace. This reflects a different understanding of how God's saving grace reaches individuals.
[2 marks per explanation: 1 for point, 1 for development]

knowledge_checks.q: Which Gospel provides the primary account of the Last Supper, arrest, crucifixion and resurrection of Jesus used in this course?
What does Acts 4:8-12 teach about salvation?
options: Salvation is found in no one else but Jesus Christ
Salvation requires performing all seven sacraments
Salvation is available through any sincere religious faith
Salvation depends on keeping the Old Testament law

knowledge_checks.q: The Protestant Reformation principle that salvation is received through _____ alone is called sola fide.
The word _____ means making amends for wrongdoing — in Christianity, how Jesus's death restores the relationship between God and humanity.
Match each event to its significance in Christian belief:
right: Jesus institutes the Eucharist/Lord's Supper as a memorial of his body and blood
Jesus dies, taking the consequence of human sin and making salvation possible
The risen Jesus returns to the Father in heaven, interceding for believers

flashcard_questions.q: Which chapters of Luke cover the last days of Jesus's life?
What did Jesus say about the bread at the Last Supper?
flashcard_questions.a: This is my body given for you; do this in remembrance of me.

flashcard_questions.q: What does penal substitution teach about the crucifixion?
flashcard_questions.a: Jesus took the punishment humanity deserved, satisfying God's justice.

flashcard_questions.q: What is the Christus Victor model of atonement?
flashcard_questions.a: The cross is where Jesus defeats the powers of sin, death and the devil.

flashcard_questions.q: What does Acts 4:12 declare about salvation?
flashcard_questions.a: Salvation is found in no other name — only in Jesus Christ.

flashcard_questions.q: What teaching about salvation does John 3:16 contain?
flashcard_questions.a: Whoever believes in Jesus will not perish but have eternal life.
Salvation by faith alone — a key Protestant Reformation teaching.

flashcard_questions.q: How many sacraments do Protestant churches generally recognise?
flashcard_questions.a: Two — baptism and the Lord's Supper (Eucharist).

flashcard_questions.q: The resurrection is foundational because Paul writes that without it, what is true?
flashcard_questions.a: Your faith is futile — you are still in your sins (1 Corinthians 15:17).
The return of the risen Jesus to the Father in heaven, forty days after the resurrection.

flashcard_questions.q: What does 'atonement' mean in Christian theology?
flashcard_questions.a: How Jesus's death reconciles humanity to God — restoring the broken relationship.

glossary_terms.definition: The final meal Jesus shared with his disciples before his arrest, during which he broke bread and shared wine as symbols of his body and blood.
The execution of Jesus by nailing him to a wooden cross; Christians believe this was the means by which God brought about salvation.
The Christian belief that Jesus rose bodily from the dead on the third day after his crucifixion.
The return of the risen Jesus to the Father in heaven, forty days after the resurrection.
The theological teaching that Jesus took the punishment humanity deserved, satisfying God's justice and making reconciliation with God possible.
How the death of Jesus reconciles humanity to God — various models exist in Christian theology.
The deliverance from sin and its consequences through faith in Jesus Christ; being brought into a right relationship with God.
The Reformation teaching that a person is put right with God through faith alone, not by earning salvation through good works.
